extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students and instructors in probability/measure-theoretic probability
extracted.subtask_description: Foundational definitions, theorems, and examples for measure-theoretic probability: probability spaces, measures, distribution functions, random variables, and basic measurability/closure properties. Suitable as a reference or textbook chapter for courses in probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Probability space (Ω, F, P)
rubrics_metrics.description: A probability space is a triple (Ω, F, P) where Ω is a set of “outcomes,” F is a set of “events,” and P : F → [0, 1] is a function that assigns probabilities to events. We assume that F is a σ-field (or σ-algebra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists the σ-field properties explicitly: (i) if A ∈ F then Ac ∈ F, and (ii) if Ai ∈ F is a countable sequence then ∪iAi ∈ F. Without P, (Ω, F) is called a measurable space. Probability measures are measures µ with µ(Ω)=1; in the book they are usually denoted P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Measure (nonnegative, countably additive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure is a nonnegative countably additive set function µ : F → R with (i) µ(A) ≥ µ(∅) = 0 for all A ∈ F, and (ii) if Ai ∈ F are disjoint then µ(∪iAi) = Σi µ(Ai).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If µ(Ω)=1 the measure is a probability measure. The text emphasizes checking consequences of the measure axioms and uses these to derive standard properties (monotonicity, subadditivity, continuity from below/above).

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of measures (Theorem 1.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences of the measure axioms: (i) monotonicity: A ⊂ B ⇒ µ(A) ≤ µ(B); (ii) subadditivity: µ(A) ≤ Σm µ(Am) if A ⊂ ∪m Am; (iii) continuity from below: if Ai ↑ A then µ(Ai) ↑ µ(A); (iv) continuity from above: if Ai ↓ A and µ(A1) < ∞ then µ(Ai) ↓ µ(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketches are given. These properties are fundamental checks when constructing measures and when taking limits of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: Discrete probability spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is countable and F is its power set, a probability measure is given by P(A)=Σ_{ω∈A} p(ω) where p(ω) ≥ 0 and Σ_{ω∈Ω} p(ω)=1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special cases include uniform probabilities on finite sample spaces. The example of the astragali (ancient dice with unequal face-likelihoods) illustrates why unequal point masses are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: σ-field generated by a collection (σ(A)) and Borel σ-field
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a collection A of subsets of Ω there is a smallest σ-field containing A, denoted σ(A). For Rd the Borel σ-field Rd is the smallest σ-field containing the open sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when checking measurability: it's enough to verify preimages lie in σ(A) for a generating class A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stieltjes measure function on R and associated measure (Theorem 1.1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures on (R, R) can be defined by a Stieltjes measure function F with properties: (i) F is nondecreasing, (ii) F is right continuous. Associated unique measure µ satisfies µ((a,b]) = F(b) − F(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lebesgue measure arises when F(x)=x. The right-closed interval choice (a,b] is convenient because intersections of such intervals behave well under limits (bn ↓ b ⇒ ∩(a,bn] = (a,b]). The long proof is deferred to the appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semialgebra and algebra generated by it (Lemma 1.1.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A semialgebra S is closed under intersection and complements are finite disjoint unions of sets in S. The algebra generated by S, denoted ¯S, consists of finite disjoint unions of sets in S and is an algebra (field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sd, half-open rectangles (a1,b1]×...×(ad,bd] form a semialgebra. One extends set functions from S to ¯S by additivity over finite disjoint unions as a step toward building σ(S).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending measures from semialgebra to σ-algebra (Theorem 1.1.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If µ is defined on a semialgebra S with µ(∅)=0 and satisfies finite additivity on finite disjoint unions and countable subadditivity (µ(S) ≤ Σ µ(Si) when S = ∪_{i≥1} Si), then µ extends uniquely to a measure on the algebra ¯S; if the extension is σ-finite it further extends uniquely to a measure on σ(S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is technical; the text provides Lemma 1.1.10 to help verify the countable subadditivity condition. The full proof is in the appendix (Carathéodory-style extension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for multivariate distribution functions (Rd)
rubrics_metrics.description: For F : Rd → [0,1] to define a measure via rectangle differences, require: (i) nondecreasing (componentwise), (ii) right continuous, (iii) appropriate limits as coordinates → ±∞, and (iv) positivity of alternating sums over finite rectangles: ∆_A F ≥ 0 for all finite rectangles A (where ∆_A F = Σ_{v∈vertices} sgn(v) F(v)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A counterexample shows (i)–(iii) alone are insufficient (can produce negative atom mass). Theorem 1.1.11 asserts existence and uniqueness of the probability measure on (Rd, Rd) with µ(A) = ∆_A F for finite rectangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Random variable / random vector (measurable map)
rubrics_metrics.description: A real-valued function X on Ω is a random variable if for every Borel set B ⊂ R we have X^{-1}(B) = {ω : X(ω) ∈ B} ∈ F. If the codomain is Rd (d>1) X is a random vector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator functions 1_A for A∈F are basic examples. The σ-field generated by X is σ(X) = {{X ∈ B} : B ∈ S} and is the smallest σ-field making X measurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of a random variable (pushforward measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a random variable, it induces a probability measure µ on (R, R) by µ(A) = P(X ∈ A) = P(X^{-1}(A)). The distribution function is F(x)=P(X ≤ x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checking countable additivity on the image follows from disjointness of preimage events. Distribution functions characterize probability laws on R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of distribution functions (Theorem 1.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any distribution function F satisfies: (i) F is nondecreasing; (ii) lim_{x→∞} F(x)=1 and lim_{x→−∞} F(x)=0; (iii) F is right continuous; (iv) F(x−)=lim_{y↑x} F(y) = P(X<x); (v) P(X=x)=F(x)−F(x−).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs rely on set inclusion relationships of events {X≤x} and standard measure continuity properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: any F with (i)-(iii) is a distribution (Theorem 1.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F satisfies nondecreasing, limits at ±∞, and right continuity, then there exists a random variable whose distribution function is F. Construction: on (0,1) with Lebesgue measure define X(ω) = sup{y : F(y) < ω} (inverse-transform construction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the inverse transform sampling method: generate U∼Uniform(0,1) and set X=F^{-1}(U) to obtain distribution F. The text gives the key identity {ω : X(ω) ≤ x} = {ω : ω ≤ F(x)}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density / absolutely continuous vs singular vs discrete distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A distribution F is absolutely continuous if F(x)=∫_{−∞}^x f(y) dy for some density f with f≥0 and ∫ f =1. It is singular if the measure is singular w.r.t Lebesgue measure. It is discrete if supported on a countable set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: uniform(0,1), exponential(λ), standard normal (density given but no closed-form F). Cantor distribution is singular (supported on Cantor set). Point mass and countable mixtures give discrete distributions. The text warns densities need not exist (singular examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal tail bounds (Theorem 1.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bounds are useful for estimating tail probabilities of the standard normal (e.g., P(χ ≥ 4)). Proof uses change of variables and simple inequalities on the integrand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating pathology and variety of distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples include Cantor distribution (singular), dense discontinuities built from rationals (F(x)=Σ α_i 1_{[q_i,∞)}), and usual discrete examples (point mass at 0, Poisson/Bernoulli/Geometric deferred to later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples illustrate that distribution functions can have dense sets of discontinuities, singular components, or purely atomic mass; useful for understanding decomposition into discrete, absolutely continuous, and singular parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurability check via generator (Theorem 1.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If {ω : X(ω) ∈ A} ∈ F for all A in a collection A and σ(A) = S (i.e., A generates S), then X is measurable (i.e., X^{-1}(B) ∈ F for all B ∈ S).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical choices: for real-valued X take A = {(−∞, x] : x∈R} or A={(−∞, x) : x∈Q}; for Rd use rectangles with finite endpoints or open sets. This is the standard technique for proving measurability of functions built from simpler ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: σ-field generated by a random variable (σ(X))
rubrics_metrics.description: σ(X) = {{X ∈ B} : B ∈ S} is the smallest σ-field on Ω that makes X measurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact is used when conditioning or discussing information generated by a random variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure properties of measurable maps and random variables
rubrics_metrics.description: If X:(Ω,F)→(S,S) and f:(S,S)→(T,T) are measurable then f∘X is measurable (Theorem 1.3.4). If X1,...,Xn are random variables and f:(Rn,Rn)→(R,R) is measurable then f(X1,...,Xn) is a random variable (Theorem 1.3.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollaries: scalar multiples and algebraic combinations (sums, products) of random variables are random variables (Theorem 1.3.6 for sums). For sums, show {X1+X2 < a} is Borel. Useful generating classes: continuity of f implies measurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sup/inf/limsup/liminf and almost sure limits are measurable (Theorem 1.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Xn are random variables then inf_n Xn, sup_n Xn, limsup_n Xn and liminf_n Xn are random variables. The event Ω0 = {ω : lim_n Xn(ω) exists} is measurable. If P(Ω0)=1 we say Xn→X almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs reduce threshold events to countable unions/intersections of events {Xn < a} or {Xn > a}. Extended real-valued random variables (taking ±∞) are allowed by equipping R* with the Borel σ-field.
